Worth reading this and asking yourself one simple question: 

If Jensen had given up and had zero shot at returning, why bother getting verified just to write a long post on X? You don't fire a public warning shot like that unless you plan to fight.

Traditional Chinese strategic thinking actually explains that exact move. Before launching a formal proxy fight, you first need to establish a just cause (师出有名).

You state your principles openly, give the board a graceful path to negotiate, and only then decide whether to escalate. 

$NVDA #BringJensenBack

quoted.text:
🚨🚨Jensen’s chances of returning: 37.36% (source: me)

Why did Jensen go out of his way to post something hinting at a return on X? He even got a blue check from Elon so he could write a long post there. Honestly, that was the part I couldn’t understand. So I’m just going to throw out some speculation of my own. 

Take it lightly, call me an idiot and feel free to ignore it.

Could the reason for Jensen’s PR move on X have been to rally support from some institutions, employee shareholders and retail investors around his own stake, and put forward board candidates willing to appoint him CEO again?

According to this year’s filing, Jensen’s disclosed stake was 3.58%. The same document listed BlackRock at 7.43% and Vanguard Capital Management at 7.31%. If Jensen is trying to use his stake as a starting point to build shareholder support, these institutions would be the first he would need to persuade.

The final move Jensen has in mind is probably a proxy fight, going through the formal process to solicit votes from other shareholders. NVIDIA’s directors have to stand for election every year. Even the directors currently opposing his return ultimately need shareholder votes to keep their seats.

That’s why I think this post may have been a signal that he was launching a public campaign in earnest, putting a little pressure on the board and starting to persuade shareholders. Simply making his intention to return public could complicate the process of finding a successor. A new CE

posts.name: Jonkoo Capital
posts.text:
Just woke up and went through the $NVDA earnings call transcript. It’s insane.

Interim CEO Colette Kress opened with: 
“Our momentum is real.”
She wasn’t kidding. 

Here’s what they said:
Guidance
• They raised FY28 revenue growth to ~75%, up from 70%, on a bigger FY27 base. That’s roughly $740B of revenue next year
• Q4 is guided to $130B
• Colette said Q4 is the bottom for gross margin, and they expect 72–73% in FY28

Vera Rubin
• Nearly $20B of revenue in its first quarter of shipments, the fastest product ramp in NVIDIA’s history
• Hyperscalers brought Rubin into production in about a month, half the time Grace Blackwell took
• Rubin Ultra comes next year and Feynman in 2028

Pricing power
• They said Hopper GPUs are being recontracted at up to 2x their original price
• B300 rental rates are up 60%+ since launch
• Every hyperscaler and neocloud they serve is running NVIDIA compute at full utilization

Demand is everywhere
• Networking alone did $21B+ in the quarter
• Sovereign AI revenue more than tripled y/y
• Physical AI is on track for $25B+ this year
• They expect CPU revenue and enterprise revenue to each more than double in FY28
• Cloud industry backlog is $2.5T, up from $2T three months ago

Neocloud financing, the part bears focus on
• Neocloud commitments are $32B, and total guarantees are $118B, including $105B of credit support for the OpenAI campus
• A new sentence in the CFO commentary says neocloud commitments only take effect if those neoclouds secure their own financing
• Stacy Rasgon asked whether that was new. Colette said nothing changed: they added it for clarity, and if a customer’s build-out stalls or is delayed, NVIDIA’s guarantee falls away
• On financing from here, they said they’ll be disciplined and selective, especially as other sources of capital come into the market
• Priority order: prepayments to suppliers first to unlock more supply, then land, power and shell. Investment-grade customers can also prepay to help fund builds
• They stressed that all customers get the same pricing. When allocating supply, they look at whether the customer’s power, shell, capital and offtake are ready

NVIDIA isn’t the lender of last resort for the neoclouds. The guarantees only kick in once the customer has raised its own money, and NVIDIA is pulling back as other capital shows up. That takes a lot of air out of the “circular financing” bear case.

Capital returns
• A record $28B returned last quarter
• They plan to use the remaining ~$227B buyback authorization by the end of FY28 and return all excess free cash flow

Leadership
• The board hired Heidrick & Struggles for the CEO search and said it won’t rush it
• Customers, suppliers and partners have all backed the company, and TSMC’s leadership was in their offices this week

This came one week after the CEO resigned.

At ~$155, $NVDA trades at about 9x the earnings their own outlook implies.

The market is pricing in the end of growth, but the company just raised its guidance.

posts.name: Patrick Moorhead
posts.text:
$MSFT Ignite came down to two words: cost and context. @Microsoft told customers Copilot does what ChatGPT and Claude do for less, while running their models and plugging its context into both. The model is now a component. That's the architectural disconnection between the model and every other stack layer I flagged in July.

What was announced:
- Copilot: Home, Office in Copilot and Managed Runtime GA. Code GA in December. Autopilot and Workspaces in Frontier, Today in private preview
- Microsoft IQ: GA, no new SKU. Work IQ plugin in ChatGPT, Fabric IQ connectors for ChatGPT and Claude in preview
- Models: seven, by Microsoft's count. MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot, Microsoft-Decision-1.1 GA, and MAI Licensed Weights so trusted customers can run a Microsoft model in their own Azure environment
- Copilotforce with @salesforce: 38+ sales skills in Copilot, public preview
- Agent 365: over 50M agents registered. Business Analytics and spend forecasting in Frontier
- Silicon: @Arm-based Cobalt 200 VMs GA, up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100, per Microsoft
- Security: Microsoft Perception GA, core Integrated SOC in Defender GA

My callouts:
1/ Cost was the keynote. @JasonTAndersen was in the room and heard that word more than any other. Microsoft's chart: $30 a month for an everyday Copilot user vs $81 for ChatGPT Enterprise and $205 for Claude Enterprise. Its advanced-user numbers matter more: $96 vs $149 vs $299. Moving to that user, with 20 agentic workflows a month, raises the Copilot bill $66 and ChatGPT's $68, by my math. Against ChatGPT, Copilot's edge is everyday use bundled into the seat, not cheaper agents. MAI Code 2 at 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's coding performance for about 40% of the price is also Microsoft's number. The direction is still right: the cheapest correct answer wins.
2/ Context is the moat. Microsoft will take the context layer even where it doesn't own the chat window. Salesforce coming into Copilot says the same thing from the other side, and it keeps control of its data and permissions. The model labs want the work surface. They can now reach Microsoft's context. They still don't own Entra, Teams, Outlook and SharePoint.
3/ Agents need CPUs, as I said in October. Microsoft says Cobalt becomes a significant share of new Azure compute capacity in 2027, next to Maia 300 for inference. Own models on own silicon is the margin lever Microsoft needs to make agents cheaper, not just seats.

Still missing: an updated paid Copilot seat count, how many customers pay for agents by usage, and credit burn for Autopilot and Code. A lot of this is still Frontier or preview. CFOs still need the number.

posts.name: Black Panther Capital
posts.text:
Mornings. I’ve been revisiting my investment thesis on $AAOI following yesterday's announcement.

(LONG WRITE-UP HERE)

And honestly, my view of management’s capital allocation is changing.

Let’s look at the bigger picture.

1. The latest dilution

On November 17, AAOI announced a new $550M at-the-market (ATM) equity offering.

This comes shortly after completing its previous $600M ATM programme, which generated approximately $588M in net proceeds.

To be clear, the new $550M is an authorization. They don’t have to sell all the shares immediately.

But the timing raises questions.

At the November 16 closing price of $45.16, a fully utilized $550M programme would represent approximately 12.2M additional shares.

That’s roughly 13.5% more shares compared with the illustrative existing share count in the prospectus.

And this is where I think shareholders need to pay attention.

2. The expansion is enormous

AAOI isn’t just buying a few machines and expanding production.

They’re building an entirely larger manufacturing operation to capture the demand for high-speed optical connectivity.

Some important numbers:

• $928.8M in outstanding equipment and facility construction commitments as of September 30.

• $200M new credit facility announced October 30.

• Up to $194.4M in annual raw material purchases under a new supply agreement.

• Up to $40M in required supplier prepayments.

• $102.25M spent acquiring three buildings at Hightower Business Park in Houston.

That’s a substantial amount of capital being committed.

And it explains why management wants access to additional financing.

3. What about buying the land instead of leasing?

Interestingly, I actually like this decision.

AAOI initially leased the three Houston buildings with purchase options and subsequently exercised those options.

I see the strategic logic.

Manufacturing facilities are long-term infrastructure assets. Owning them provides greater control over expansion, modifications and future occupancy costs.

And unlike rent, the purchase creates an asset on the balance sheet.

But buying the buildings doesn’t automatically create additional production capacity.

The return depends on what they install inside them, how quickly they can bring the facilities online and how much profitable output they generate.

The property isn’t the problem.

The total capital allocation strategy is what deserves scrutiny.

4. Management: The good and the bad

I don’t want to overlook what management has achieved.

Q3 2026:

• Revenue: $269.9M, up 127% YoY.
• Datacenter revenue: $155.6M.
• GAAP net income: $6.3M.
• Six consecutive quarters of record revenue.

That’s real operational progress.

But there are some warning signs.

Gross margins haven’t expanded alongside revenue. Q3 GAAP gross margin was 28.2%.

The company has also acknowledged construction and power-related delays in its US expansion.

And despite the tremendous revenue growth, operating cash flow remains under pressure.

I want to see the business become increasingly self-financing.

Not increasingly dependent on issuing shares.

5. So why am I becoming more critical of management?

Because I think there’s a difference between investing ahead of demand and committing so much capital that shareholders continuously have to finance the execution.

Management has raised substantial equity capital this year.

They’ve secured manufacturing facilities, ordered equipment, entered into major supply agreements and expanded their capacity ambitions.

I understand the strategy.

The AI infrastructure opportunity is enormous, and being underprepared when customers need capacity could be far more expensive than expanding early.

But what happens if construction takes longer than expected?

What happens if demand shifts, customer orders are delayed or margins remain compressed?

Shareholders absorb the dilution while management still has to deliver on the investments.

That’s the risk.

6. What I want to see next

Five thin

posts.name: Cheddar Flow
posts.text:
$NVDA earnings summary:

Q3 revenue hit $115.8B, crushing the $109.3B estimate and topping even the highest analyst forecast of $114.9B. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.68 vs. $2.47 expected, with a 74.9% gross margin. That makes 17 straight quarters beating consensus and 15 straight above the top of Nvidia's own guidance. 

Data center did the heavy lifting at $107.6B (est. $101.9B), split between hyperscalers ($60.1B) and AI clouds, industrial & enterprise ($47.5B), with Vera Rubin alone adding nearly $20B quarter over quarter. Compute & networking ($106.0B), graphics ($9.8B) and edge computing ($8.2B) all came in ahead of estimates too.

The outlook is just as strong. Nvidia guided Q4 revenue to $127.4B–$132.6B (~$130B midpoint) vs. $125.3B expected, with 71–72% gross margins and about $10.7B in operating expenses. That guide assumes zero China data center revenue, even after $2.4B in Hopper shipments there this quarter. Commitments jumped to $390B from $279B in Q2, neocloud agreements total $32B, and the board added $150B to the buyback, leaving $227.3B to deploy through FY2028. The AI build-out isn't slowing down.

Grosse journée sur la TECH

Je vous ait résumé ce qu'il s'est dit lors du premier jour de TomorrowX :

1. AMD : Lisa Su dit que la demande dépasse l'offre malgré les contrôles à l'export. Elle parle d'un cycle générationnel plutôt que cyclique, sans phase de digestion, même si le ROI revient dans chaque discussion avec les clients. La salle a trouvé qu'elle n'avait pas dit grand-chose de nouveau.

2. SpaceX et Anthropic : le CFO de SpaceX, a priori, n'est pas inquiet sur la demande de compute et pense qu'Anthropic en aura besoin de beaucoup plus. Pour financer 10 GW, il n'y aurait pas besoin de lever des fonds propres : le cash-flow et la dette suffiraient. Beaucoup y ont vu le talk le plus intéressant de la journée. Le bémol : quand on annonce plus de demande, le marché ne monte plus, il pose des questions sur le financement. En face, Gerstner a surtout fait la promo d'Anthropic, tout en estimant qu'environ 500 MW d'inférence pourraient lui suffire l'an prochain.

3. Druckenmiller : il est en mode préservation du capital, ni long ni short actions, et juge le marché un peu survendu. Il voit Warsh plus hawkish que prévu, des spreads de crédit écartés et un second semestre 2027 potentiellement négatif pour l'économie. Pour lui, les infrastructures ne sont qu'un trade tactique : la valeur viendra des usages comme la santé et la cyber, avec des labs qui vendront des tâches plutôt que des tokens.

4. Un peu de signal : Vercel est passé d'environ 600 M$ d'ARR début octobre à environ 700 M$, soit +100 M$ en cinq semaines grâce au code agentique. Le CEO de Fireworks cherche toujours du compute et voit encore une forte pénurie. Cerebras dément tout froid avec OpenAI et attend une hausse du CA du T3 au T4, puis en 2027. Michael Dell ne change pas d'avis sur le buildout.

5. Le camp bear : Gavin Baker vendrait MU et plus largement le groupe capex. Plusieurs participants pensent que les profits glissent vers les labs d'IA, et que les infrastructures et les semis deviennent la commodité, puisque c'est la relation avec l'utilisateur qui compte. La salle était à moitié vide, ce que certains lisent comme le signe que le point bas n'est pas encore fait

Compliqué de se positionner ici, je pense que les signaux sont brouillés, on sent clairement que le sentiment est mauvais 

On a l'impression que toutes les caisses ont été vidé pour aller sur Anthropic et que tout le monde attend ce soir, le juge de paix $NVDA

$SLS Regardless of if you know anything about science and statistics, I feel like everyone should ask the following question and use their gut instinct/common sense to try to understand the answer:

Why was this the shortest conference call I can recall ever for a successful clinical trial? Let alone one that is apparently transformative? The start of the section after forward looking statements was at the 1:18 mark and ended at 5:00. The remaining ~10 minutes was self-congratulations. That's 15 minutes in total. For context, $ABVX had a nearly 50-minute call to discuss their original induction data. The average call is between 30 and 75+ minutes post pivotal data.

The $SLS call was:

1) Here is the data in slide format and basics on trial design (essentially just the press release granularity) (~3 minutes 40 seconds).

2) Thank you everyone for supporting us, it's been such a long road to get to this point (~10 minutes)

3) Goodbye. (5 seconds)

This was the single pivotal moment where, as management said themselves, they've been slogging at for over a decade. This is also a way to directly (and legally) promote to KOLs, investors, etc about why this is so transformative, your opinion on market opportunity, the timelines to submit, and strategic interest color. Why would you spend as little time as possible on the call?

Does that make any sense, at all? What would be the motives for not wanting to talk about it any further, or not wanting to take any questions from analysts who were primed to also congratulate you and give you very softball questions?

I don't think management is clueless. Their past fireside chats were 20-30 minutes each. Is it possible that they thought the risks of saying anything more than what was on the slides, or of being asked a question that would put them into a challenging position, was not worth the reward of saying anything further about the trial, the drug, the opportunity, or their strategic goals?

posts.name: IvanaSPEAR
posts.text:
Are NVIDIA — “the Bank of AI” concerns justified?

Over the past week, concerns about off-balance-sheet commitments tied to AI infrastructure have intensified.

Headline estimates of $3-4 trillion are raising eyebrows, but the high-level totals tell us little about how big the risk is or where it sits.

Not every off-balance-sheet commitment is a loan waiting to go bad. These obligations have very different purposes and economics.

1. Purchase commitments: building capacity.

Committing to equipment or projects under construction is not, by itself, a red flag. The questions are whether companies have the cash flow to meet those commitments, and whether the investments will earn attractive returns.

Google stands out in this chart for its purchase commitments, well ahead of Amazon and Microsoft.

This implies upside to Google capex.

2. Leases not yet commenced: renting capacity.

Hyperscalers can build or lease. A company with fewer construction commitments may have more future lease obligations. Neither route makes growth free.

Microsoft looks more weighted toward leasing than building.

Meta stands out as one of the more aggressive builders + lessees… not surprising given their ambitions and progress in AI Agents.

Clearly, whoever has internal use cases (Google and Meta) has more confidence to build, which is a positive.

3. Guarantees and backstops: underwriting someone else’s business.

This is where the “Bank of AI” concern becomes more legitimate.

Nvidia is putting its balance sheet behind customers’ expansion, helping them secure financing while taking on additional risk itself.

Two arrangements stand out:

▪️ OpenAI: Up to $105 billion of guarantees for a data center in Ohio - declining as lease payments are made.

▪️ CoreWeave: A capacity backstop initially valued at $6.3 billion, requiring Nvidia to buy qualifying unsold computing capacity through April 2032.

Note that Nvidia's guarantees and backstops are less than 1x LTM EBITDA, and the company has only $30B in debt… hardly a stretched balance sheet.

The debate also leaves out the other side. Nvidia’s equity investments have done pretty well.

▪️ $30B OpenAI investment is worth $45 today at the latest Open AI valuation.

▪️ $10B xAI investment that became SpaceX was worth $21 billion at June 30.

▪️ $10B Anthropic investment would be worth ~$40B at the proposed IPO valuation.

That adds up to roughly $50B+ in gains on just these 3 deals over <2years.

The Bank of AI may not be doing so bad after all.

posts.text: There are few reliable predictive signals in the market, but one of them is volatility. High volatility tends to predict future volatility. On any random day, $SPY has a 4.8% chance of a move larger than 2.4% (up or down), and a 25% chance of one in any given two-week period. You could buy 100 shares of $AMD right now for about $49,160.

Or you could sell a $400 cash-secured put expiring Jan 15, 2027 and get paid about $1,868 to wait.

Here's how this plays out:

1. AMD stays above $400 by expiration - you keep the $1,868 premium. That's a 4.7% return on capital in 59 days (28.9% annualized).

2. AMD drops but you still like it - roll the put down and out to collect more premium and lower your entry.

3. You get assigned - your real cost basis is $381.32 per share. That's a 22% discount from where the stock trades today.

Why I like this setup:

- Q3 revenue hit a record $13.4B, up 45%, and data center revenue nearly doubled to $8.5B
- AMD guided Q4 revenue to about $17B, roughly 66% growth
- Helios racks are shipping, and Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle are already running workloads on them
- The stock is about 25% below its 52-week high of $658.52
- IV rank is 79, so premiums are rich, and the next earnings report is expected after this put expires

The $400 strike is about 19% below the current price at roughly a 0.20 delta. The plan is to close it at 50% profit.

If the stock drops well below your strike, you're buying shares at a loss relative to market price. Only sell puts on stocks you genuinely want to own.

Not financial advice. I share these for education.

posts.text:
Michael Dell, founder and CEO of Dell Technologies $DELL, at TomorrowX Summit.

Gavin Baker of Atreides Management opened with an interesting question.

Over the past five years, Dell has outperformed every Magnificent Seven stock except NVIDIA.

Why haven't other server competitors achieved similar results?

Michael Dell pointed to the company's longstanding foundation in servers, storage, and data center infrastructure.

Long before the AI boom, Dell had already established deep relationships with national laboratories and enterprise customers.

That foundation is now a major advantage in the AI infrastructure race.

Then Gavin asked an even more interesting question.

"What if we're at peak AI right now?"

Michael Dell strongly disagreed.

For that to happen, the fundamental thesis behind AI would have to be wrong.

His reasoning was fascinating.

Humans are naturally curious. We constantly want to discover more and solve problems we haven't yet figured out.

Biology, materials science, and scientific research still have countless unanswered questions.

And AI could drive much of the progress in these fields.

He expects AI to become increasingly efficient while delivering substantial benefits to the US economy.

What I find particularly interesting is that Dell doesn't build frontier AI models.

Regardless of who wins the AI model race, computing infrastructure remains essential.

While Wall Street continues debating peak AI capex, the founder of one of the world's largest server suppliers seems convinced that AI is still in its early stages.

Perhaps the more important question isn't when AI infrastructure investment peaks, but how much scientific progress AI has yet to unlock.

Now, the technology.

1. CPUs still matter.

While CPU market growth has been in the single digits, Lisa suggested that momentum has been strengthening recently.

Even in the GPU-driven AI era, CPUs remain essential.

2. Democratizing AI.

Lisa emphasized her passion for solving problems from an engineer's and scientist's perspective.

For AMD, democratizing AI means making powerful computing resources accessible to more researchers and developers.

She highlighted supercomputing, national laboratories, healthcare, and scientific research.

The bigger vision is AI that can improve real lives, including those of our families.

3. Why Xilinx and FPGAs matter.

Lisa highlighted the strategic importance of AMD's Xilinx acquisition.

In her words, 1 + 1 is better than 3.

Building AMD's full technology roadmap requires more than CPUs and GPUs.

Modern data centers need CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and heterogeneous computing architectures working together.

AMD isn't simply trying to compete with NVIDIA GPU against GPU.

It's building a broader computing platform spanning CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and supercomputing.

A different approach to the future of AI infrastructure.

posts.name: Daniel Koss
posts.text:
This is the WORST AI sentiment I've ever seen on X.

Never before have I seen so many long-term bulls capitulate in public.

But I also see a ton of bears abusing the negative sentiment to spread completely false information to increase the panic.

Let's take $NBIS as the X poster child for this and compare the mind-numbing disconnect between fact and narrative.

1) "Nebius is burning money like there's no tomorrow."

I've read so many people on here saying different versions of the same thing: $NBIS is burning about $27B in 2026 to only generate $3B in revenue. Spending $9 for each $1 you make is not a sustainable business model.

I mean, first we gotta just appreciate how freaking absurd these people are 😂 I almost respect how dishonest they can be with a straight face (who knows, maybe they are smiling while writing this).

Of the ~$27B that Nebius spends in 2026, most does not go toward monetized capacity that comes online this year. The investment is mostly used to build and monetize data centers. These projects take quarters to years.

And here's what's much more important: they then generate revenue for years.

So the ~$27B they spend in 2026 is very likely to generate at least $65B+ in revenue over the 5-year life of the GPUs alone. $65B, not $3B. But don't sweat the details, that's just a 21.7x difference 🙃

2) "Who cares how fast they grow, the business isn't profitable = not sustainable."

Just straight up wrong. Their unit economics are in a strong uptrend and their payback period is now down to 1 year and 7 months. That means it takes them very little time, by any traditional infrastructure standard, to be profitable on their investments, and after that they are making massive profits for 3+ years.

3) "None of that matters. The business is way too capital-intensive. Dilution and debt will eat all gains for investors."

Even before last quarter that simply wasn't the case, because, surprise, management does the math on how much profit they expect from these investments and whether it's higher than the cost of the financing or the loss of gains from dilution.

And in just one quarter, prepayments on new deals went from 50-60% to more than 100% of the associated capex, paid upfront by customers.

In other words: on new deals, customers are now financing the buildout for Nebius! Non-dilutive financing, and not even debt.

Personally, I think the ROI will be so high that they should actually also take on debt much more aggressively than they are right now. But the fact is they are being very conservative compared to $CRWV, $ORCL and the actual neoclouds.

4) "Nebius is artificially inflating their profitability by assuming way too optimistic depreciation timelines."

Once again, the opposite is reality.

Nebius is at the most conservative end of the industry. $NBIS depreciates servers over 5 years. Only $AMZN has also moved some of its AI servers to 5. Everybody else assumes longer: $META 5.5 years, $GOOGL, $ORCL and $CRWV 6 years, $MSFT up to 6.

5) "Prices will crash as supply catches up."

You can guess... Yep, once again, the opposite is happening.

The issue for data center companies, now including Nebius itself, was that bringing supply online, especially power at third-party sites, is significantly harder than they assumed. That's why you're seeing all these delays.

posts.text:
BREAKING: A cybersecurity firm used AI to uncover a critical security flaw in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages.

The bug, dubbed “Java4Shell,” was found by start-up Calif in OpenJDK, the core software that runs Java programs. Researcher Quang Luong used OpenAI’s Codex coding agent to find the flaw in about an hour, then build a working attack in about two more, for less than $200 in computing costs. Calif rated it 9.2 out of 10 for severity.

The flaw sits in Java’s Base64 decoder and can be triggered by sending just 64 “A” characters followed by a single “=.” That can corrupt the computer’s memory, potentially letting an attacker take over a server or expose sensitive data, similar to the Heartbleed bug. Calif demonstrated a working break-in on Keycloak, a widely used login system, and says tools like Jira, Confluence and Jenkins are also at risk.

Java runs at 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Calif estimates, and is used by banks, hospitals and governments worldwide. “This is such an unlikely and serious flaw,” computer scientist Toby Walsh told the BBC, because Java is designed to handle memory safely.

Oracle and OpenJDK have released fixes.

quoted.text: This whole Nvidia situation is such a huge lesson in board composition for founders

posts.name: Balaji
posts.text:
All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

A 27% loss, yet saving is still considered safe.

UK inflation has jumped to 3.6%, the highest level in a year. The spotlight is now on the Bank of England, and markets are pricing in further rate hikes.

What usually gets lost in the noise is how inflation steadily erodes our purchasing power. Over the 16 years since the Great Financial Crisis, UK inflation has averaged 3%, or 50% above the Bank of England's official target. 

Over that same period, the average rate "offered" by UK financial institutions was just 1%. That leaves a massive gap between what your hard-earned pounds earn in a savings account and what rising prices take away.

The result is harsh: since 2011, UK savings have lost 27% of their purchasing power. Is that really what a central bank is after?

Charts like the one below are everywhere, and with government debt historically high and budget deficits uncomfortably large, the gap between yield and inflation is unlikely to close. 

Savers with the capacity and endurance should therefore look for better ways to preserve and grow their wealth. Saving is not a virtue, as the hard but objective data below show.

Insider buying activity is getting HOT 

Corporate insiders have shown reasonably elevated open-market buying in recent months of 2026, particularly from August through mid-November. 

Dollar volumes of purchases reached roughly $1.4- 2B in some of those months (with November still incomplete at ~$900M+ so far), higher than quieter stretches earlier in the year such as June-July. 

Open-market insider buying especially when done by executives or directors, or in clusters is traditionally viewed as a bullish indicator because insiders have better information and are putting their own money at risk.

Recent insider buying supports the idea that some companies look attractive to their own executives and directors, which is a constructive note.

posts.name: Damnang
posts.text:
🚨🚨Jensen’s chances of returning: 37.36% (source: me)

Why did Jensen go out of his way to post something hinting at a return on X? He even got a blue check from Elon so he could write a long post there. Honestly, that was the part I couldn’t understand. So I’m just going to throw out some speculation of my own. 

Take it lightly, call me an idiot and feel free to ignore it.

Could the reason for Jensen’s PR move on X have been to rally support from some institutions, employee shareholders and retail investors around his own stake, and put forward board candidates willing to appoint him CEO again?

According to this year’s filing, Jensen’s disclosed stake was 3.58%. The same document listed BlackRock at 7.43% and Vanguard Capital Management at 7.31%. If Jensen is trying to use his stake as a starting point to build shareholder support, these institutions would be the first he would need to persuade.

The final move Jensen has in mind is probably a proxy fight, going through the formal process to solicit votes from other shareholders. NVIDIA’s directors have to stand for election every year. Even the directors currently opposing his return ultimately need shareholder votes to keep their seats.

That’s why I think this post may have been a signal that he was launching a public campaign in earnest, putting a little pressure on the board and starting to persuade shareholders. Simply making his intention to return public could complicate the process of finding a successor. A new CEO would have to consider the next board election and their relationship with the founder as soon as they take office. Jensen may have been trying to make sure they could not ignore him before a new leadership team became firmly established.

At least the NVIDIA employees I spoke with really wanted him to return. The question now is whether institutional investors also decide that Jensen’s return is in their own interests. If that support translates into actual shareholder votes, the directors will have to factor in their own reelection as well. Perhaps Jensen has made the first move toward building a board that would appoint him CEO again.

This is just factually wrong. A bank deposit is not a promise to deliver "state money". It's a promise to deliver you money. But they can explicitly refuse to deliver you cash and that's the only kind of state money you can request in the USA. 

Page 26 of Bank of America's Deposit agreement specifically says they can refuse to give you cash. 

"We may place restrictions on when and how you make large cash withdrawals. We may refuse to honor your request if you do not comply with these restrictions, or if we believe that honoring a request to withdraw cash or cash a large check or similar item would cause an undue hardship or security risk."

So this comment is just factually wrong. The liability isn't to provide you with cash. it's to provide you with the value you're owed, in the form they deem reasonable.

We've never seen an environment where you had the gap we have now between monetary policy and inflation. TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10AM TO 10PM on 11/17/26

Huang spoke for himself for the first time since resigning, owning the personal mistakes and saying he would return if the board decided it was best. Hours later the board chair answered on the earnings call: the board unanimously accepted the resignation and does not intend to reinstate him, and a search firm is retained. The Wall Street Journal reported a new SEC investigation into whether Nvidia disclosures misled investors. The board created a national security and export control oversight committee. Earnings beat and guidance rose, with no 10-Q filed with the release. The December House interview dates are now reported as agreed, and Muddy Waters disclosed a short with an expressly unverified identity question at its center.

HUANG SPEAKS, THE BOARD ANSWERS

• Jensen Huang issued his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, in his own post on November 17, 2026, read in full. He said verbatim: "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
• He thanked supporters, noted an outpouring of calls from Nvidia employees, investors, business partners and customers for him to return as CEO, and stated: "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." No prior claim in the record records any public statement by Huang himself since the resignation; the comeback reporting was third party.
• Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened the third quarter earnings call on the evening of November 17, 2026 by stating on the record: "On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." The statement was carried verbatim or near verbatim the same evening by CNN, Engadget, USA Today and Reuters, all read in full; no full earnings call transcript was obtained.
• Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress declined to take questions on Huang's resignation or the ongoing investigation, saying the board will communicate further when appropriate. Jones said the board had retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the permanent CEO search, considering internal and external candidates, thoroughly and as quickly as possible without expediting past the right person, and expressed the board's full confidence in Kress.
• This hardens the position in the record: the board's no return position was previously carried only as anonymous sourced reporting on November 16. The chair has now stated it himself, on the record, unanimously, hours after Huang put the return decision to the board.

A NEW SEC PROBE

• The Wall Street Journal reported on November 17, 2026 that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia, according to people familiar with the matter. This is the Journal's reporting, on a single source chain, with no SEC statement, filing or comment recorded and Nvidia not quoted responding.
• The Journal describes a civil investigation whose focus could not immediately be learned but includes whether the company's disclosures misled investors, in the wake of Huang's resignation. It notes Nvidia had denied earlier this year that Huang had an unusual or unexpected relationship with Alice Huang, then an executive at Singapore based Megaspeed, and that Nvidia last year changed how it discloses international chip sales, eliminating the disclosure

posts.text:
🚨 Anthropic’s IPO will not be just another listing. 

It will create a new public benchmark for the entire AI trade.

Here is what changes once Anthropic begins trading.

1. Software gets a public competitor for capital

A liquid company valued above $1T, generating roughly $68B in annualized revenue with approximately 900% net revenue retention, would put a daily market price on the idea that AI is taking spending from traditional application software.

IGV is already leading the market lower.

Anthropic gives investors a direct way to trade that disruption.

2. The chip impact cuts both ways

Roughly $130B in cash, plus potentially $100B in new capital, would make Anthropic one of the best-funded compute buyers in the world.

That strengthens the credibility of supplier backlogs. These commitments would be supported by cash, not merely guarantees or circular financing structures.

But Anthropic distributes its compute spending across Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs.

That benefits custom silicon exposure at GOOGL and AVGO while potentially weakening NVIDIA’s pricing power.

The reported $26B of supplier stock purchases will also be viewed by some investors as vendor financing.

3. The AI scarcity premium shrinks

Until now, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers were among the only liquid ways to own the AI buildout.

That is changing.

SpaceX raised $86B in June. Anthropic is next. OpenAI is expected to follow.

Together, these companies could introduce hundreds of billions of dollars in new AI equity for the market to absorb.

That creates real competition for capital and could pressure existing AI holdings long after the IPO fundraising is complete.

4. The opening print resets the sector

Anthropic’s book is reportedly about six times oversubscribed. That demand doesn’t come from new money. It comes from funds trimming the AI names they already own.

If the debut holds, it supports private AI valuations, but it also proves investors can now own AI directly instead of through chips, cloud and software. The proxies lose their scarcity premium either way.

If the deal breaks, the pressure spreads across the full complex, especially companies whose valuations depend on continued infrastructure spending.

Suppliers get the spending in both cases. The rest of the AI complex has to absorb the new supply in both cases.

We are not predicting which outcome occurs.

But once Anthropic starts trading, the market will have a new price for AI demand, AI disruption and AI risk.

The entire complex will be valued against it.

The earnings implication is less straightforward than the revenue implication. High-value GPUs and other purchased components can inflate system revenue without a proportionate increase in gross profit. Annual platform transitions also require inventory planning, engineering resources and working-capital funding. Neither NVIDIA’s 75% fiscal 2028 growth outlook nor its system-level margins should be transferred directly to these suppliers.

The near-term catalysts are Rubin shipment execution, customer acceptance and early DSX POD orders. The longer-duration opportunity is a greater share of repeatable, integrated AI-factory production. The most useful cross-portfolio distinction is between companies selling scarce proprietary components or qualified infrastructure and companies passing expensive components through larger system invoices. Both can grow rapidly, but their margins, funding requirements and cash conversion can diverge materially.

posts.text:
Macro frame:

CEOs are accountable to the market, so they have to be at least somewhat honest, or else the product just doesn't work.

Modern Western politicians are typically liars, but they do need to get elected, so extremely flagrant matters sometimes lead to accountability.

Finally, journos lie for a living, but they lie in packs, all at once, together — the school-of-fish strategy — so it's hard to single one out. Who coulda knew? Therefore they have the least accountability. Their owners are also a kind of CEO, but unlike the typical CEO, their news product actually is lies and/or based-on-a-true-story.

All that is reflected here. 

Fundamentally, I submit that's what's actually going on. Most people can't keep twenty people in their head, all the journos spreading lies. But they can keep one face in their head. So they scapegoat that guy, putting all the weight on him, forgetting everyone targeting him, magnifying his faults.

It only works if he is actually important in some way, a leader who they can blame. Girardian scapegoating if you will.

THERMAL ALERT: KERCH STRAIT BRIDGE, RUSSIA

SITE
• Kerch Strait Bridge (Crimean Bridge), Russia and occupied Crimea, 19 km road-and-rail crossing of the Kerch Strait; the navigational arch span crosses the Kerch-Yenikale Canal, the main deepwater passage between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea
• Russia's only road and rail link to Crimea and its main military logistics artery to the peninsula
• The bridge is not a refining or energy site: this analysis runs on a post by sentdefender (11/17/26 3:42 PM EDT) claiming a missile strike collapsed the arch and roadway

DETECTION
• FIRMS thermal pull over the bridge corridor (lat 45.24 to 45.37, lon 36.44 to 36.62), 11/15/26 to 11/17/26, VIIRS SNPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and MODIS: zero detections
• A structural collapse with brief impact fires is a weak thermal target, so the null carries little weight either way; the event is established by wire reporting and verified imagery, not by thermal satellite
• Sentinel-2 imagery from 10/26/26 shows the arch span intact over the canal, protective booms in the water; the first clear post-event pass is still pending

CONFIDENCE
• Event real at the site: HIGH, 95%+
• Cause (Ukrainian drone and missile strike): HIGH, 90-95%
• Damage (road arch and span collapsed, road link severed; rail arch damaged, rail bridge standing): HIGH, 85-90%
• The sentdefender video as evidence of the strike: LOW, under 10%
• Rationale: claimant and target state agree on the event, and Reuters verified the imagery Kyiv published. The residual uncertainty is in the details (weapon mix, repair time), not the event. His video, by contrast, is an Exilenova+ watermarked montage set to an Eminem track; frame by frame it shows distant night explosions and one fire filmed through industrial pipe racks, a plant, not a bridge. No bridge, arch, or collapse appears in it.

CORROBORATION
• X: the primary material is Zelenskyy's own posts with video, verified by Reuters; Ukraine's General Staff stated on X that the arch and span collapsed and no vehicle can cross; sentdefender relayed the claim this afternoon, after the wires; Russian monitoring channels, via NOELreports, warn of a possible further FP-5 attack tonight
• Officials: Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed damage and suspended traffic, with rail resumed on one track today (Interfax); the Investigative Committee called it a terrorist act; Aksyonov confirmed the attack and reported two killed elsewhere in Crimea; Peskov promised a repair plan
• Web: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg News and the FT all carry the collapse, the SBU's seven-stage operation account (Palianytsia drones on the road section, Neptune and Ruta and FP-5 on the rail section, Flamingo the final blow; seven of nine missiles that hit were Ruta), and Ambrey's note that the fallen arch blocks the Kerch-Yenikale Canal; Russia's MoD claimed 1,441 drones intercepted overnight, the largest barrage of the war, and this was the second strike on the bridge in two nights
• Status: VERIFIED; road section destroyed at the arch span, rail damaged but operating on one track. Kyiv's year-plus repair estimate for the fallen roughly 6,000-tonne structure is a claimant figure, unverified

WHY IT MATTERS
• Crimea logistics: with the road link severed and rail on one track, fuel and military supply into Crimea shifts to ferries and the land corridor; Crimea fuel tightness, with retail restrictions already across six-plus Russian regions, gets worse. That supports the product-tightness side of the refining picture even as the paper crack sells off
• Azov transit: debris in the canal impairs Azov port flows (Rostov, Azov, Taganrog) days after a FIRMS-verified fire at the Azov oil depot; the campaign is now working the whole Azov-Crimea logistics chain, and a third attempt tonight is openly warned of on Russian channels
• Timing: two days before the Putin-Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen, a spectacular escalation that cuts against the peace-process repricing pressuring cracks this week

posts.name: IP Capital Partners
posts.text:
Existe um problema em negócios lucrativos e asset light: depois de algum tempo não há mais para onde reinvestir. O caixa se acumula e não encontra destino (a não ser o bolso do acionista). Ao longo da história da Berkshire, a companhia foi hábil em possuir dentro do seu conglomerado negócios asset light como também asset heavy, de forma que o caixa gerado num negócio mais maduro e lucrativo fosse direcionado para um com maior necessidade de emprego de capital.

A Berkshire tem, por exemplo, na See’s Candies um dos negócios mais rentáveis que já comprou: marca forte, preço premium e pouco capital empregado. O dinheiro entra e não encontra destino dentro da operação. Para um investidor comum, sobra de caixa é um bom problema. Para a Berkshire, com capital crescendo em escala, isto virou um tema a ser resolvido. Onde alocar o que a See’s não absorve?

A resposta foi a BNSF, uma ferrovia. Um negócio intensivo em capital, perene e capaz de absorver bilhões de dólares de uma só vez.

Agora troque See’s Candies por pesquisas na internet. Ben Thompson, do Stratechery, fez muito bem essa analogia. O search do Google é talvez o modelo de negócio mais perfeito já construído: custo marginal baixo, escala em todas as direções, altamente lucrativo, dominante e gerador de caixa. No entanto, com menores oportunidades para reinvestir.

Já o negócio do Google Cloud tem características distintas. Necessita de muito capital para crescer, oferece bons retornos, entretanto, inferiores ao negócio de search. Porém o mercado endereçável é potencialmente maior.

Essa combinação de negócios da Alphabet é portanto similar à lógica da Berkshire: O fluxo de caixa de negócios altamente lucrativos, asset light, é direcionado para divisões mais intensivas de uso de capital. Do search ao Google Cloud.

Um negócio extraordinário, capaz de crescer o seu valor intrínseco por décadas, não é necessariamente o mais lucrativo. É o que consegue reinvestir, em escala, o caixa que produz.

Fonte: Invest Like the Best | What Happens When the AI Boom Runs Out of Money with Ben Thompson

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.

Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single person. When those teams form companies, specialize, and coordinate across an entire economy, you get civilizational progress.

Coinbase is building the financial rails and accounts for the agentic economy. We’re also building the marketplace where agents can find, hire, and pay one another (see follow on post below).

Every company can now sell its own specialized open-weight model, trained on its proprietary data, that beats the frontier on narrow, high-value tasks. Builders can shop the marketplace and assemble teams of these specialized agents in minutes.

Freedom of choice and real competition in the agentic market will create far better outcomes for everyone.

SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen says SpaceX will fly its next-gen direct-to-cell satellites next year, aiming for true 5G service from space to phones in the first half of 2028

"Over 13 million people getting connected now. And so when we looked at that, we thought that that is very exciting. Maybe that ramps to hundreds of millions, but how do you get to the 3 billion? You gotta do it with your handset, with your cell phone."

"And so we then started down the path of flying our first generation constellation, flew 600 satellites to do proof of concept, and so now you get text only service. It's already helping from an emergency perspective around the world in multiple locations, but it was really just a proof of concept."

"And now we're starting to work on the satellites that we really start flying next year, which are our next generation direct to cell, or DTC satellites. It's a separate constellation from the broadband business."

"And so we're gonna fly those satellites next year with the goal in the first half of 2028 of turning on a true 5G quality service from space to your cell phone. No change required to the hardware."

"We bought spectrum, actually two versions of spectrum now, the mid band from EchoStar and then the low band that we just announced not too long ago. So we have all the pieces in place from a regulatory perspective in the United States for that."

quoted.text:
Anthony, the "spy" story appears to be as fake as Russiagate. Here are the facts as I understand them.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnera

posts.name: Raoul Pal
posts.text:
Back in 2013 I was living in Spain, watching banks across southern Europe fail one after another. The European debt crisis was in full swing and it got bad enough that I bought a generator and filled the cupboards with tinned food.

Then Cyprus did something no country had done before. Its banks were going under, and instead of rescuing them, the authorities made the depositors pay... anything over €100,000 in your account was swapped for shares in a collapsing bank. They called it a bail-in. People lost their savings overnight.

That was the moment it dawned on me... you don’t actually own the money in your bank account. The bank does. And it can do what it likes with it.

So I went looking for somewhere to keep money that nobody else had a claim on, and that search led me to Bitcoin. I bought my first at around $200.

It started as my escape hatch from a broken banking system and eventually I understood it as the life raft out of the debasement trap.

It’s where the crypto chapter of The Everything Code picks the story up... with a generator and a cupboard full of tinned food.

posts.name: Nicole Perlroth
posts.text:
I haven’t lived here in awhile, but I see no other way to answer the hundreds of texts/DMs asking me if the world is, indeed, ending. 

In the span of six days, we’ve experienced;

11/12 — Microsoft outage
11/13 — Nationwide FAA ground stop
11/16 — Major US banking disruptions
11/17 — NSA’s classified internal network goes down

We need far more analysis of why so much is breaking at once. I don’t want to get out over my skis here, and what I am hearing does not contradict the messaging that most of this is the result of screwy updates. 

But stepping back, the dots are starting to form a collective picture. We are seeing: 

• An explosion in severe and critical vulnerabilities, with AI accelerating discovery to 3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year. This is collectively being referred to as “vulnageddon” or “the vulnpocalypse.”

• Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS. AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.

• Powerful AI-enabled offensive tools like ARTEX have been thrown into the hands of every third tier nation state, cybercriminal and digital arsonist, which logically creates havoc. 

• This creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates, increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.

• Pressure to just “AI everything” means we are rolling out automated AI tooling on top of brittle infrastructure that can’t support it. 

My generation grew up in an extraordinary period of technological stability. We worked our way up the software stack, abstracting away layer after layer, until we lost a fundamental understanding of how the underlying systems actually work.

We were told to “move fast and break things.” VCS told us to celebrate the idea that “software would eat the world.” Now we’re telling ourselves we can simply “roll out AI” across everything, as though nothing underneath will buckle.

We never stopped to ask: SHOULD WE?

Should we be digitizing every last nook and cranny of our companies, infrastructure, healthcare, homes, cars, bodies, lives? Especially when the complexity, interdependence, and fragility we were introducing overwhelmed our ability to understand/secure/maintain the systems we built?

Nobody every asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?

We are now entirely dependent on software systems that almost nobody understands end to end, that increasingly few people can repair, and that attackers can now probe at machine speed. We are hearing that incident response firms, the 911 for breach victims, are backlogged six months. Even those paid on retainer lack the bandwidth to triage every incident. The cavalry is disappearing.

We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability. 

“Software Beirut” is an incredibly apt analogy.  We are in for a period of cascading failures, whether triggered by attackers, bad updates, or our own accumulated complexity.

This, I’m sorry to say, is just the opening chapter.

posts.name: Bruce Richards
posts.text:
Yesterday I joined Carl Quintanilla and Melissa Lee on CNBC's Squawk on the Street:

- Nvidia's backstops, circular financing and vendor financing support the neoclouds and their VC companies that rely on this funding, with a question as to whether they will continue to provide this funding. Hyperscalers have an abundant access to capital, while non-IG companies face materially higher funding costs. Nvidia's Q3 results will be strong, but forward guidance is more uncertain.

- The Commerce Department announcement and proposed the MATCH Act raise questions about the degree by which Nvidia chips flows through intermediaries in Singapore, Malaysia and Taiwan to Chinese controlled companies. Up to 30% of sales goes to this region, so the question remains is this at risk?

- Wall Street expects $1.5T of AI and data center capex in 2028. If it lands 30% lower, near $1T, while still a large number, it's below expectations, yet considerably healthier for credit markets, giving investors a chance to digest this supply.  Remember roughly 2/3rds of the CapEx spend is financed in the public and private credit markets. Looking beyond 2027, equity and credit analysts have adopted a more conservative forecast in subsequent years.

- Crowding out is omnipresent. AI and data centers are competing for fixed income allocations, just as the US government does when it runs a 6% deficit. Both raise R*, and the cost of capital for smaller companies and those with lower credit scores.

- Less frenzy in the capital markets is healthy. Deflating the AI bubble rationalizes capital allocation and sets the sector up for long-term success. Earlier this year, everything got funded, which was not healthy.

- HY spreads are unchanged this month despite equity volatility. BBs trade near 200 bps, while CCCs yield 18%, which is a huge historical anomaly. CCCs have only traded this wide during recessions and periods of great stress, at during those periods, BBs traded ~500–800 bps spreads. Within the CCC sector, 50% trade near a 35% yield while the other 50% of CCCs trade close to a 10% yield. So, within the CCC sector, there is a K-shape to credit, or a K within the K. Many of the former CCCs will likely default in two to three years, with stress concentrated in TMT; while the stronger CCCs are generally high-yielding, better credits. Doing your credit work is essential.

- Capital allocators should strongly favor Private Credit in this market. Higher for longer provides lenders with extra yield. The Fed will continue to tighten, so the yield goes up on floating-rate debt. Direct lending should have a good vintage. Asset-Based Lending secured by hard assets can deliver 10% to 12% returns with low volatility and limited identifiable AI impact on assets such as aircraft, shipping, rail cars, home mortgages and senior housing. With the need for capital solutions and growth capital, Opportunistic Credit is well positioned.

JPMORGAN WARNS LEVERAGED-LOAN DEFAULTS COULD MORE THAN DOUBLE IN 2027

JPMorgan forecasts U.S. leveraged-loan defaults will surge to 4.5% in 2027 and 4.75% in 2028, up from 1.96% in October.

Companies facing AI disruption, elevated borrowing costs and looming debt maturities are particularly vulnerable, especially in software and technology.

Of the $862 billion in debt maturing between 2027 and 2029, 46% carries a B3-or-lower credit rating.

Meanwhile, high-yield bond defaults are projected to rise more modestly to 2.75% in 2027.

The outlook signals mounting stress in corporate credit markets.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. Brad Gerstner says only 26% of Anthropic's compute this year went to serving paying customers, and the rest went mostly to training

"Everybody thinks, oh my God, they gotta spend so much money to serve up Claude, to run these agents. Only 26% of their compute budget this year went to generating $100 billion in revenue. That's 500 megawatts."

"They had two gigawatts of compute this year, and only 25% of it went to serving this all up. The vast majority of it goes to training, which, to me, says, wow, next year the consensus forecast is another 100 billion of revenue. They only need 500 megawatts."

"So when you hear all of this concern about data centers and this and that, they just don't need that much compute to hit their numbers for next year."

"Of course, they want a lot more. Why do they want a lot more? Because they know we're in the foothills of the singularity, of super intelligence. They want to be the first ones to get there. It takes a lot of training to get there, but this shows why it's such a good business model."

posts.text:
Brad Gerstner says only 26% of Anthropic's compute this year went to serving paying customers, and the rest went mostly to training

"Everybody thinks, oh my God, they gotta spend so much money to serve up Claude, to run these agents. Only 26% of their compute budget this year went to generating $100 billion in revenue. That's 500 megawatts."

"They had two gigawatts of compute this year, and only 25% of it went to serving this all up. The vast majority of it goes to training, which, to me, says, wow, next year the consensus forecast is another 100 billion of revenue. They only need 500 megawatts."

"So when you hear all of this concern about data centers and this and that, they just don't need that much compute to hit their numbers for next year."

"Of course, they want a lot more. Why do they want a lot more? Because they know we're in the foothills of the singularity, of super intelligence. They want to be the first ones to get there. It takes a lot of training to get there, but this shows why it's such a good business model."

TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/17/26

The window brought the first official government account of the Megaspeed investigation. The Commerce and Justice Departments issued a joint statement setting out their timeline and putting the Justice Department in the lead on the criminal investigation, while making no allegation against Nvidia or Jensen Huang and saying nothing on the Entity List question. On the return question, reporting now has the board not considering bringing Huang back, the opposite direction from the comeback reporting in the record. President Trump and Vice President Vance both cast doubt on the claim that Alice Huang was a spy. In the Senate, the Commerce Committee's ranking member put four alleged export control failures in writing to Secretary Lutnick, and a Republican senator introduced a bill to force a listing decision on Megaspeed within 30 days. The shareholder case against Nvidia and Huang widened by amended complaint.

THE GOVERNMENT SPEAKS

• On November 16, 2026, the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation, posted by the Commerce Department's official account and issued expressly to address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting. The statement was read in full from the official post and verified word for word against a verbatim carriage and against Reuters reporting of the same statement.
• The official timeline: after identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no sell list.
• Also in June 2025, Bureau of Industry and Security agents, together with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed chief executive Alice Huang. Following that enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
• The departments state they will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred, credit Secretary Lutnick's Commerce Department and Attorney General Blanche's Justice Department, and cite seventeen defendants charged across six semiconductor smuggling investigations under the Trump administration.
• The statement makes no allegation against Nvidia or Jensen Huang, and it does not address the Entity List question. It is the first official Commerce or Justice Department statement in the record on the investigation's posture and timeline. Its account of the Commerce probe does not use the word suspended, which is the word Senator Cantwell's letter, filed in this same window, uses for what happened when the Justice Department took the criminal investigation.

THE BOARD IS NOT DISCUSSING A RETURN

• CNBC reported on Monday, November 16, 2026 that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as chief executive and is not in discussions to do so, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity. The Washington Post, citing a person familiar with the board's thinking, and the Financial Times reported the same position the same day.
• CNBC reported the board is focused on its investigation into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets, an investigation CNBC reported is led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.

posts.name: Mohamed A. El-Erian
posts.text:
A thought ahead of the Nvidia earnings call later today:
It's not just about earnings, actual and prospective.
With the economy and markets so leveraged to AI, what happens to Nvidia’s financial structure is systemically important.
Characterized as the “central bank of AI,” the company sits at the center of a web of interdependent funding involving equity stakes, vendor financing, and compute commitments, often involving financially vulnerable firms.
The contract terms are not public and, as such, durability under stress is uncertain.
IF, and it’s an IF, the system is severely stressed, possible spillovers include capex, employment, economic activity, and fair value.
With no reliable baseline forecast available, potential outcomes span a wide distribution: ranging from no change and an orderly adjustment absorbed by strong balance sheets to a disorderly unwind that tightens AI credit conditions and dampens wider corporate spending.
More to follow.
#economy #markets #ai #nvidia @nvidia

posts.name: The Kobeissi Letter
posts.text:
It's officially Nvidia's earnings day.

Today's earnings report and call will likely be the most watched earnings event in history.

We are watching two key things:

1. Do executives show any willingness to reinstate Jensen Huang

2. What has CHANGED from a business perspective

As of now, considering the information over the last 48 hours, we believe there is an <20% chance that Jensen returns.

Any indication that the probability is higher would be strongly bullish for the stock.

But, if not, then what has changed for Nvidia? With or without Jensen, this company remains one of the best businesses in the world.

We are looking to see if the company still expects revenue growth of 70%+ in FY2028, as management previously indicated.

We also look for any changes to AI infrastructure spending, demand for Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips, and the company's relationships with its largest customers.

If the fundamental outlook remains intact, then investors must ask: Does Jensen Huang's departure justify the -$750 billion in lost market cap?

We believe the market has already priced in a significant portion of the uncertainty surrounding Jensen's departure.

At the same time, the long-term AI infrastructure investment cycle remains intact, and Nvidia continues to sit at the center of it.

The burden is now on management to demonstrate that the business can continue executing at the same level without Jensen Huang.

More to come after earnings.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Legally, reserves are liabilities of the 12 Federal Reserve Banks, which are federally chartered corporations with member bank shareholders. They aren't liabilities of the Treasury or of "the State."

Congress drew this line itself. Section 16 of the Federal Reserve Act makes Fed notes obligations of the United States. Reserves never got that language. Courts have treated the Reserve Banks as independent corporations too, not federal agencies (Lewis v. United States, 9th Cir. 1982).

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
The reserves part is wrong. A depositor has no claim on reserves. Reserves are the bank's asset sitting at the Fed, and a depositor is an unsecured creditor of the bank. I can tell my bank to pay you. I can't tell it to move reserves. How my bank squares up with your bank is its business, whether that's reserves, netting, a correspondent balance or an overnight loan.

And you don't get reserves either. You get a deposit at your bank. That's where the payment ends for both of us. UCC 4A is explicit about this. My payment to you is complete when your bank accepts the payment order, and my debt is discharged at that point. If your bank accepted before it got paid and my bank then blows up, that's your bank's loss, not mine and not yours.

So there are two settlements here. Customers settle in deposits. Banks settle with each other in reserves, or net down until there's a residual they settle in reserves. Same bank payments don't touch reserves at all. Reserves are the final settlement asset between banks. They aren't how customer payments get settled. So you literally cannot demand state money.

You keep saying that I only rises when C falls. That is simply not true. You are confusing increases and reductions in the nominal amounts of GDP components with increases and reductions in their shares of GDP.

To the extent that structural transfers that shift income from households to subsidize investment lower the household income and consumption shares of GDP, the combined share of investment and net exports must rise. There is no way around this. If nominal consumption rises less quickly than nominal investment and net exports rise, however, the only way to balance it is with slower growth in production, in which case investment and net exports can decline even as their shares of GDP rise.

More oil amateur hour from @DrJStrategy 

He sees a 36% drop in crack spreads and declares an oil glut.

A 3-2-1 crack spread measures refining margins, not crude supply-demand balance.

quoted.text:
Crack Spreads Are Dropping Like a Stone

The US 3-2-1 crack spread, the refiner’s margin for turning crude into gasoline and diesel, has collapsed 36% in six weeks, from $ 65.56 a barrel on 9 October to $ 41.90 today. It’s at a new low and still falling.

That tells you the glut has moved downstream. Fat margins pulled refiners into running flat out, and now product markets are swamped. Gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude. That’s exactly what wholesale RBOB futures, down 20%, and $ 3.78 at the pump were already signalling.

Collapsing margins also mean more relief is coming. Retail prices lag wholesale by weeks, so the pump hasn’t finished falling. Every 10 cents off gasoline takes about 9bp off headline CPI. November is shaping up for a negative headline print, and in March the war spike drops out of the year-over-year math.

This is a supply glut, not a demand problem, and it’s doing the Fed’s job for it. Hiking 1% into a collapsing refining margin isn’t vigilance. It’s insanity.

Paul Tudor Jones: I Went Broke Three Times, Now I Focus on What I Can Lose

In the past two weeks, we've been playing as big as we've ever played before, because of the fact we think we know what's going on. Like right now, I'm watching the currencies, I'm watching crude, I'm watching stocks and bonds. They're all interrelated. The whole world is simply nothing but a big flowchart for capital. And if I start getting hurt in, for instance, stocks or bonds, then I'm going to make a total portfolio adjustment just because of the fact I might not like the way the numbers are going over the course of the day.

I've personally gone bankrupt, not declared bankruptcy, but lost everything I had and had to borrow from friends three times in nine years that I've been in the business, where I'd go sit in the park and just sit there and just go, "I can't believe this. You know, this is the end. This is the end of my life."

Where you want to be is always in control, never wishing, always trading, and always first and foremost protecting your ass. That's why most people lose money as individual investors or as traders, because of the fact they're not focusing on losing money. They need to focus on the money that they have at risk. How much capital is at risk in any single investment they have? If everyone spent 90% of their time on that, or the 90% of their time on pie-in-the-sky ideas about how much money they're going to make, then they'd be incredibly successful investors.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
You misunderstand how bank lending can add to NFA. For example:

A firm borrows $100k to invest and pays it out as wages and dividends. Households end up with $100k in deposits and no debt, a $100k gain in net financial assets. The business sector carries the matching debt but owns a new productive asset. No government deficit needed. Household NFA is created whenever another sector runs a deficit, and businesses borrowing to invest is the main way that happens in a healthy economy. This has an even larger multiplier on househokd net wealth if firms are revalued higher.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Crack Spreads Are Dropping Like a Stone

The US 3-2-1 crack spread, the refiner’s margin for turning crude into gasoline and diesel, has collapsed 36% in six weeks, from $ 65.56 a barrel on 9 October to $ 41.90 today. It’s at a new low and still falling.

That tells you the glut has moved downstream. Fat margins pulled refiners into running flat out, and now product markets are swamped. Gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude. That’s exactly what wholesale RBOB futures, down 20%, and $ 3.78 at the pump were already signalling.

Collapsing margins also mean more relief is coming. Retail prices lag wholesale by weeks, so the pump hasn’t finished falling. Every 10 cents off gasoline takes about 9bp off headline CPI. November is shaping up for a negative headline print, and in March the war spike drops out of the year-over-year math.

This is a supply glut, not a demand problem, and it’s doing the Fed’s job for it. Hiking 1% into a collapsing refining margin isn’t vigilance. It’s insanity.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Retail sales kept moving forward in Oct, but were weighed down by loss in big ticket spending on vehicles, furniture and appliances. Still core retail sales, which go into GDP, outpaced inflation. They were propelled forward by more paychecks & wealth effects - people have leverage financial assets by borrowing against their value and pay cash & home equity lines of credit  - even as wage gains under paced the rise in inflation. 

Resilience that does not resonate for too many continues to be the theme. 

The @federalreserve survey of consumer finances, which came out Oct 9 for 2025, showed top 10% accounted for 32% of consumer spending and approx half of discretionary - the Fed excluded the top 400 wealthiest on Forbes list, as it skewed the data too much. That was prior to inflation this year, which further skewed & concentrated gains. 

We added paychecks in Oct, which helps buoy spending even as individual lived experience feels as though they are losing ground. Wages fell short of inflation for seventh consecutive month. Almost as many months below as above inflation since expansion began. 

Inflation is higher for low-& middle-income households than affluent households due to composition of what they buy. Shelter, food, utilities, health care. That is important as it means they are losing more ground than averages suggest. You can tell a worker they are making more with benefits but when those gains include higher copays & costs, and wages are lagging inflation, it doesn’t feel like better compensation to workers. 

Moreover, the concept of keeping up with the Jones’ is real. 

Consumers will resist with everything in their power reductions in living standards - drain saving, take on debt. The @federalreserve SCF showed 20% of families behind on debt payments before inflation surge this year. Consumer will also resists reductions in the pace at which they accumulate stuff - hoarding is almost hardwired into our psyche. 

A good way to think about it is that if you are stuck in a slow lane of traffic and a vehicle next to you speeds fast, it feels as though you are moving backwards. That is all too real in an economy with high inequality and a billionaire class that echoes the Gilded Age. 

So, we get spending & the momentum of 2026 is for the moment still in tact. But, hard to have those gains resonate. And fragilities under the surface.
