posts.name: Nikhil Krishnan
posts.text:
Seems like local politicians may be turning on hospitals?

Since healthcare represented a huge part of employment in a given state, a lot of local politicians would fight on the side of their local providers. But I have a feeling that’s changing as more realize that it’s at the expense of other jobs in the state.

There’s a paper by Zack Cooper and the “f*** monopolies” squad that used IRS data to see what happens after hospital mergers jack up prices, and every 1% price increase leads local non-healthcare employers to cut payroll and headcount by ~0.4%.

A jobs program doesn’t work if you LOSE jobs from other employers not hiring.

Companies are choosing where to close locations or open up new ones based on local healthcare costs. Indiana is an interesting example of this:

“We have plants all over the country, and whenever we’re talking about opening a new one, do you know what I say? I say, ‘ABI,’” according to the Indy Star. The executive elaborated: “Anywhere but Indiana. 

On average we pay $2,200 for every worker’s emergency room visit in Indiana. In Michigan it’s $800. The difference there is the profit margin on one” - Becker’s Hospital Review

Indiana is now taking on the hospitals in the state and trying to cap how much they can charge employers or risk losing their non-profit status. You are starting to see many more states exploring these kinds of hospital price caps as their own state health plans are bearing enormous costs.

As voters themselves lose trust in their local hospitals, politicians also see an opportunity to use that to their advantage.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
A 1% Hike Into a Gasoline Glut Is Insanity

St Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem wants a full percentage point of rate rises before spring. That is how policy mistakes are made.
He describes “persistent strong demand”. The data say otherwise. US petrol prices are up 37 per cent on a year ago, while core CPI is 2.6 per cent. This is a war-driven supply shock, and a rate rise does not drill a barrel or move a tanker through Hormuz.

The shock is already reversing. Wholesale petrol futures are 20 per cent off their October high, and pump prices are at their lowest since July. The IEA now has supply running ahead of demand. Inventories rose 52mn barrels in October, and 2bn barrels sit at sea. November headline CPI is set to fall month on month. In March, the war spike drops out of the annual comparison and headline inflation falls by roughly three-quarters of a percentage point. By May it is near 2 per cent, with no help from the Fed.

Musalem warns of inflation becoming “entrenched”. Markets disagree. One year breakevens are below 2%. The 5y5y forward inflation expectation is 2.15 per cent, below its long-run average, and the Fed has never launched an aggressive tightening cycle with expectations that low.
His real-rate arithmetic is backwards, wrong and reckless. We should expect more from the Fed. This is extreme incompetence!

As headline inflation falls, real rates rise on their own. Add a full point of hikes and policy becomes crushingly tight just as inflation collapses.

So is his 1970s analogy. The real lesson of that decade is that central banks should not tighten into supply shocks.

This is not vigilance. It is driving by the rear-view mirror at full speed.

posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
AI data-centre: 100% moratorium improbable, modest slowdown likely and it will elongate the cycle (and the selloff has already priced a lot in)

Post-midterm noise has focused on local ballots, state pauses and talk of tighter rules on new data centres. Legitimate friction exists: power, water, permitting and community pushback are real constraints. However, a near-total U.S. halt is improbable as it will send the US into an immediate recession.

AI is a strategic priority; economic and geopolitical costs of freezing buildout are high. Much near-term capacity is already permitted or under construction.

Private land + evolving power solutions (gas, nuclear, efficiency) + international options provide outlets.

No federal ban has material traction; impact is more delay and higher cost than cancellation.

Base case from banks: some 2028 projects slide to 2029. This elongates the AI capex cycle rather than derailing it. Positives include:

1) Smoother supply-demand rebalancing (less boom-bust risk for the supply chain).

2) Better utilisation and pricing power for compute.

3) Improved credit outlook and more sustainable multi-year spending.

4) Hyperscalers still guiding strong near-term capex; and they will likely become FCF +ve

The aggressive selloff in AI infrastructure names (picks-and-shovels, semis, related industrials) has already discounted substantial slowdown risk. Multiples have compressed hard while order books and guidance have stayed firm. This looks more like a positioning/sentiment reset than a fundamental end of the cycle.

Quality AI infrastructure exposure still looks attractive if demand holds. Best to own companies with strong balance-sheets, high margins, FCF and real backlog. http://alphatarget.com

posts.text: The strongest evidence for Robin's point sits in the oil market. Tankers are being hit near Hormuz almost every day and crude still can't rally. When a shooting war at the world's main chokepoint can't lift prices, demand is already weakening. CPI will show that months from now, and the Fed is setting policy on the old picture.

quoted.text:
What's unfolding in the US is a policy mistake. The Fed is tying itself in knots over a backward-looking CPI while oil prices are tumbling. The result is that real rates and the Dollar are going through the roof, even as the growth picture is weakening...
https://robinjbrooks.substack.com/p/the-fed-is-making-a-terrible-mistake

posts.name: Gabriel Senise
posts.text:
The hawkish hold is what's keeping the Dollar tight, rather than a broad risk-off. The advanced-economy leg has stayed firm, and the EM Dollar hasn't confirmed a wider move. 

If policy starts looking through the shock, that G10 leg is what should retrace with oil.

quoted.text:
Oil prices are down 20% since October, yet the Fed insists on being hawkish. That's backward-looking. The result is real rates are the highest in over 20 years. The Fed has to go back to looking through supply shocks or it'll push the US into recession...

posts.name: Marhelm
posts.text: Japan is pushing for an Asian version of the IEA, with regional oil stockpiles and deeper Gulf cooperation. The Hormuz crisis has changed the energy security conversation. Asia no longer wants to be caught short of barrels.
